definition: An alignment of three celestial bodies, such as the sun, earth, and moon, in a roughly straight line.
exampleSentence: During the eclipse the children learned they were witnessing a rare syzygy of sun, moon, and earth.
etymology: From Late Latin 'syzygia', from Greek 'syzygos' ('yoked together'); a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The slender figure-eight curve traced by the sun's position in the sky when photographed at the same time of day across a whole year.
exampleSentence: He bolted his camera to the balcony and, photographing the noon sun weekly, slowly captured a perfect analemma.
etymology: From Latin 'analemma', from Greek 'analemma' ('support, pedestal'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A faint oval glow in the night sky directly opposite the sun, caused by sunlight scattered back from interplanetary dust.
exampleSentence: Far from any town, with the moon down, she could just make out the ghostly gegenschein overhead.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Gegenschein' ('counter-shine'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of a pale greyish-yellow, parchment, or fawn colour.
exampleSentence: The old letters had faded to an isabelline hue that made them look centuries older than they were.
etymology: From the proper name Isabella, with the OED noting the colour-sense predates the popular legend; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A pale grey-green colour, named after a type of glazed Chinese pottery.
exampleSentence: She painted the nursery a soft celadon that seemed to hold the calm of early spring.
etymology: From French 'céladon', after a character in d'Urfé's pastoral romance 'L'Astrée'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A deep saffron-to-mustard yellow pigment made from gum resin.
exampleSentence: The autumn ginkgo turned a blazing gamboge that lit up the whole grey street.
etymology: From New Latin 'gambogium', from 'Camboja' (Cambodia), source of the resin; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The paragraph mark (¶) used in writing and typesetting.
exampleSentence: He clicked the little pilcrow icon to reveal all the hidden formatting in his document.
etymology: Alteration of Middle English 'pylcrafte', ultimately from Greek 'paragraphos'; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary and Collins.

definition: A nonstandard punctuation mark combining a question mark and an exclamation point (‽).
exampleSentence: His incredulous text—"You did what‽"—called out for an interrobang.
etymology: Coined 1962 by Martin K. Speckter from 'interrogation' + 'bang' (printers' slang for the exclamation mark); a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The hash or pound symbol (#).
exampleSentence: Long before it was a hashtag, the telephone company politely called it the octothorpe.
etymology: A 20th-century American coinage of disputed origin, 'octo-' for its eight points; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The tiny dot placed over a lowercase i or j.
exampleSentence: In her elegant handwriting even the tittle over each i was a perfect little circle.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'titulus' ('inscription, heading'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A slanting line (/) used to separate alternatives, mark line breaks, or denote fractions.
exampleSentence: The editor told her to replace the clumsy 'and/or' and its virgule with a clearer phrase.
etymology: From French 'virgule' ('comma'), from Latin 'virgula' ('little rod'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A symbol (÷ or †) used to mark division or, historically, to flag a doubtful or spurious passage in a text.
exampleSentence: The scribe set a small obelus beside the verse he suspected was a later forgery.
etymology: From Late Latin 'obelus', from Greek 'obelos' ('spit, pointed pillar'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An angled quotation mark (« or ») used in French and several other languages.
exampleSentence: The French novel framed every line of dialogue in graceful guillemets rather than the curly marks she knew.
etymology: French diminutive of 'Guillaume' (William), said to honour 16th-century typecutter Guillaume Le Bé; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sudden breaking-off of speech, as if the speaker were unwilling or unable to continue.
exampleSentence: "Why, if I ever catch him, I'll—" and his furious aposiopesis hung in the air more menacingly than any threat.
etymology: From Late Latin, from Greek 'aposiopesis' ('a becoming silent'); a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The insertion of a word or words into the middle of another word, as in "abso-bloomin-lutely."
exampleSentence: "Un-frickin-believable" is a cheerful piece of everyday tmesis.
etymology: From Greek 'tmesis' ('a cutting'), from 'temnein' ('to cut'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A word or form that occurs only once in an entire body of text.
exampleSentence: Translators argued for decades over the verse because the crucial term was a hapax legomenon found nowhere else.
etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th c. from Greek, meaning 'something said only once'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Writing in which alternate lines run in opposite directions, like an ox ploughing a field.
exampleSentence: The ancient inscription was carved in boustrophedon, so he had to read one line left to right and the next right to left.
etymology: From Greek 'boustrophedon' ('turning like oxen in ploughing'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The tendency to perceive a specific, meaningful image, such as a face, in a random or ambiguous pattern.
exampleSentence: It was just pareidolia, of course, but she couldn't stop seeing a startled face in the electrical socket.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Pareidolie', from Greek 'par-' + 'eidolon' ('image'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The tendency to perceive meaningful connections or patterns between unrelated things.
exampleSentence: His conviction that the lottery numbers spelled out a message was textbook apophenia.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Apophänie', coined by psychiatrist Klaus Conrad in 1958; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A painting technique of blending tones so softly that outlines seem to vanish like smoke.
exampleSentence: The Mona Lisa's enigmatic smile owes everything to Leonardo's mastery of sfumato.
etymology: From Italian 'sfumare' ('to evaporate, tone down'), related to 'fumo' ('smoke'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A painting or decorative work executed entirely in shades of grey.
exampleSentence: The chapel ceiling was a sombre grisaille that mimicked carved stone relief.
etymology: From French 'gris' ('grey'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A vivid literary description of a work of visual art.
exampleSentence: Keats's poem on the Grecian urn is the most famous ekphrasis in English.
etymology: From Greek 'ekphrasis' ('description'), from 'ekphrazein' ('to recount, describe'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A European decorative style imitating Chinese motifs and ornament.
exampleSentence: The drawing room was full of blue-and-white chinoiserie, from the wallpaper to the lacquered cabinets.
etymology: From French 'chinois' ('Chinese'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Paint laid on so thickly that it stands up in ridges from the surface.
exampleSentence: Van Gogh's stars are built from swirls of impasto you can almost feel with your fingertips.
etymology: From Italian 'impasto' ('a paste, dough'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Decoration made by scratching through a surface layer to reveal a different colour beneath.
exampleSentence: The potter finished the vase with delicate sgraffito, scoring leaves through the dark glaze to the pale clay.
etymology: From Italian 'sgraffito' ('scratched'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Metalwork shaped into relief by hammering from the reverse side.
exampleSentence: The silver bowl's rim was decorated with vines in fine repoussé.
etymology: From French 'repousser' ('to push back'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The grooved wooden plug that forms the mouthpiece of a recorder or whistle.
exampleSentence: A crack in the fipple meant the old recorder could no longer hold a clean note.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, recorded from the 17th c.; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Elaborate ornamentation of a vocal melody with runs, trills, and leaps.
exampleSentence: The soprano's dazzling coloratura in the final aria brought the house to its feet.
etymology: From Italian 'coloratura' ('colouring'), from Late Latin 'coloratus'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A rotating cage in a mechanical watch that counteracts the errors gravity introduces into timekeeping.
exampleSentence: Through the sapphire dial you could watch the tiny tourbillon turning once a minute.
etymology: From French 'tourbillon' ('whirlwind'); a headword in Collins.

definition: The end of the day; evening.
exampleSentence: At eventide the fishermen drew their boats up the shingle and lit their lamps.
etymology: From Old English 'ǣfentīd'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The early morning; dawn, when the rooster first calls.
exampleSentence: They rose at cockcrow to reach the market before the heat set in.
etymology: From 'cock' + 'crow', attested in Middle English; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The part of the day between dawn and noon; the morning.
exampleSentence: He spent the whole forenoon mending nets and was finished well before lunch.
etymology: From 'fore-' + 'noon'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A full continuous period of one night and one day; twenty-four hours.
exampleSentence: The fever broke after a single exhausting nychthemeron at the bedside.
etymology: From Greek 'nykt-' ('night') + 'hēmera' ('day'); a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A period of seven nights; a week.
exampleSentence: "I shall return within a sennight," the messenger promised, "or not at all."
etymology: Contraction of Old English 'seofon nihta' ('seven nights'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of or relating to winter; wintry.
exampleSentence: A hiemal hush lay over the fields, broken only by the crunch of frost underfoot.
etymology: From Latin 'hiemalis', from 'hiems' ('winter'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Wintry; relating to the winter or the winter solstice.
exampleSentence: They huddled by the fire through the long brumal nights.
etymology: From Latin 'brumalis', from 'bruma' ('winter solstice'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Snowy; resembling or full of snow.
exampleSentence: By morning the garden wore a niveous coat that softened every edge.
etymology: From Latin 'niveus', from 'nix' ('snow'); a headword in Collins.

definition: Granular old snow that has partly compacted on its way to becoming glacial ice.
exampleSentence: Above the treeline their boots crunched into the dense, year-old firn.
etymology: Borrowed from German/Swiss dialect 'firn' ('of last year'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A thin film of clear ice coating rock or other surfaces.
exampleSentence: A treacherous verglas on the granite slab forced the climbers to turn back.
etymology: From French 'verglas', from 'verre' ('glass') + 'glas' ('ice'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Feathery white ice crystals that form on surfaces when water vapour freezes.
exampleSentence: The hoarfrost edged every blade of grass with tiny crystalline spines.
etymology: From Middle English 'hor' ('grey, white with age') + 'frost'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A coating of opaque white ice formed when supercooled fog droplets freeze on contact with a surface.
exampleSentence: After the freezing fog, the pines on the ridge were thick with rime.
etymology: From Old English 'hrīm'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A bright halo of light around the shadow of one's own head, cast on dewy grass.
exampleSentence: As he walked across the wet lawn at dawn, a faint heiligenschein crowned his shadow's head.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Heiligenschein' ('holy shine, halo'), used in this optical sense from 1834; a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A luminous cloud or radiant halo surrounding a figure or object.
exampleSentence: The streetlamp gave her a soft nimbus of gold in the foggy dark.
etymology: From Latin 'nimbus' ('rain cloud, halo'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A radiant halo of light, especially one around the sun or moon seen through thin mist.
exampleSentence: A pale aureole ringed the winter moon, promising frost by morning.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'aureola' ('golden'), from Latin 'aureus'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A milky, shifting play of soft colours like that of an opal.
exampleSentence: The dawn sky took on a faint opalescence, pink and green bleeding into the grey.
etymology: From 'opal', from Latin 'opalus'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A tiny trace, spark, or particle of something.
exampleSentence: There was not a scintilla of evidence to support the rumour.
etymology: From Latin 'scintilla' ('spark'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To sparkle or glitter.
exampleSentence: Dew on the spiderwebs made the whole hedge glister in the early sun.
etymology: From Middle English 'glistren', of Germanic origin; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sensation of light produced without light entering the eye, as when one presses on a closed eyelid.
exampleSentence: She rubbed her tired eyes and watched the phosphenes bloom and drift in the dark.
etymology: From French 'phosphène', from Greek 'phos' ('light') + 'phainein' ('to show'); a headword in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Marked by extraordinarily vivid and detailed recall of images.
exampleSentence: With his eidetic memory he could recite the page after a single glance.
etymology: From Greek 'eidetikos' ('relating to images'), from 'eidos' ('form'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Relating to the drowsy, semi-conscious state experienced as one wakes from sleep.
exampleSentence: In that hypnopompic haze she was sure she'd heard her name called from the hall.
etymology: From Greek 'hypnos' ('sleep') + 'pompe' ('a sending away'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The eerie sense that something perfectly familiar has become strange and unrecognizable.
exampleSentence: She stared at the word until it dissolved into nonsense—a small fit of jamais vu.
etymology: From French 'jamais vu' ('never seen'); a headword in Collins.

definition: A distortion of memory, such as déjà vu, in which imagination and fact are confused.
exampleSentence: The uncanny certainty that he had lived this moment before was a flicker of paramnesia.
etymology: From Greek 'para-' ('beside') + 'amnesia'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The inability to feel pleasure in things that are normally pleasurable.
exampleSentence: The grey weight of anhedonia drained even his favourite music of its joy.
etymology: From Greek 'an-' ('without') + 'hēdonē' ('pleasure'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Feeling regret or remorse; pricked by conscience.
exampleSentence: A compunctious glance at the empty plate told her he'd eaten the last of the cake.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'compunctio' ('a pricking'), from Latin 'compungere'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Wisdom or the perfect retort that arrives too late to be of any use.
exampleSentence: Only on the drive home did afterwit supply the devastating reply she should have given.
etymology: From 'after' + 'wit', in English since the late 16th c.; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Having the power to shape disparate things into a single unified whole.
exampleSentence: He praised the poet's esemplastic imagination, which fused memory and landscape into one image.
etymology: Coined 1817 by S. T. Coleridge from Greek 'es hen' ('into one') + 'plastic'; a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The state of withering while remaining attached, as leaves that cling to a tree through winter.
exampleSentence: The young oaks kept their brown leaves all winter, a stubborn marcescence against the snow.
etymology: From Latin 'marcescere' ('to wither'); a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The unfolding or appearance of leaves; foliage.
exampleSentence: By late April the bare hedges had burst into a tender green frondescence.
etymology: From Latin 'frondescere' ('to put forth leaves'), from 'frons' ('leaf'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A winged, dry fruit such as the spinning seed of a maple or ash.
exampleSentence: The children threw maple samaras into the air to watch them helicopter down.
etymology: From Latin 'samara' ('elm seed'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The arrangement in which young leaves are folded or rolled within a bud before they open.
exampleSentence: The fern's tight spiral is a classic example of circinate vernation.
etymology: From Latin 'vernare' ('to flourish, be springlike'), from 'ver' ('spring'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A new shoot springing up from the root of a plant such as sugar cane after cutting.
exampleSentence: After the harvest the field greened again with vigorous ratoons.
etymology: From Spanish 'retoño' ('sprout'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The fraction of light that a surface reflects, especially of a planet, moon, or snowfield.
exampleSentence: Fresh snow has such a high albedo that it can dazzle you on a clear day.
etymology: From Late Latin 'albedo' ('whiteness'), from Latin 'albus' ('white'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A soft murmuring or rushing sound, as of wind moving through trees.
exampleSentence: All night she listened to the sough of the pines against the cabin wall.
etymology: From Old English 'swogan' ('to sound, roar'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The shrill, piercing sound of bagpipes.
exampleSentence: The skirl of the pipes drifted down from the castle and made the hairs on her neck rise.
etymology: Of Scandinavian origin, related to Norwegian 'skryla' ('to shriek'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To flow with a soft murmuring sound, as a small stream running over stones.
exampleSentence: The brook purled gently beside the path, cool even in the August heat.
etymology: Probably of Scandinavian origin, imitative; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A rattling, clattering noise.
exampleSentence: The brattle of hailstones on the tin roof drowned out the radio.
etymology: Imitative, chiefly Scots; a headword in Collins.

definition: Sooty; dark and murky, as if filled with smoke.
exampleSentence: The fuliginous fog of the old industrial city stained every collar grey.
etymology: From Late Latin 'fuliginosus', from Latin 'fuligo' ('soot'); a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A central point; the hub or focal centre of something.
exampleSentence: For the old scholars, the cathedral was the omphalos of the entire kingdom.
etymology: From Greek 'omphalos' ('navel, central point'); a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: An old Edinburgh warning cry shouted before slops were thrown from an upper window into the street.
exampleSentence: "Gardyloo!" came the shout, and the wise pedestrian leapt clear of the doorway.
etymology: Probably from French 'gare à l'eau!' ('beware of the water'), first known use 1622; a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Foolish talk; nonsense.
exampleSentence: He dismissed the whole horoscope as a column of cheerful flapdoodle.
etymology: An arbitrary 19th-century coinage; a headword in Merriam-Webster, Collins, and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A petty lie; pretentious nonsense.
exampleSentence: His excuse for being late was an obvious taradiddle about a runaway horse.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, recorded from c. 1790; a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A frantic or overwhelming desire for freedom.
exampleSentence: A restless eleutheromania seized him each spring, and he longed to quit the city for good.
etymology: From Greek 'eleutheros' ('free') + '-mania'; a headword in Collins.

definition: A fool or simpleton.
exampleSentence: "Don't stand there like a ninnyhammer—help me carry it!"
etymology: From 'ninny' + 'hammer', first known use 1592; a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To confuse, perplex, or fluster.
exampleSentence: The new tax form was designed, it seemed, purely to bumfuzzle anyone who read it.
etymology: Probably an alteration of 'befuddle' or 'bamboozle', U.S. dialect; a headword in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A pompous, self-important official or pretender to authority.
exampleSentence: Some local panjandrum insisted on inspecting our permits twice before letting us pass.
etymology: Coined 1755 by Samuel Foote in a nonsense passage; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A boastful and self-important little man.
exampleSentence: The strutting cockalorum lectured the room as if he'd built it himself.
etymology: A mock-Latin extension of 'cock', recorded from the 18th c.; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A cowardly braggart or rascal.
exampleSentence: He played the scaramouch all evening, boasting loudly until the first sign of trouble sent him fleeing.
etymology: From Italian 'Scaramuccia', a stock cowardly clown of the commedia dell'arte; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A person who frequently shifts opinions or vacillates in argument.
exampleSentence: As a politician he was a notorious whiffler, agreeing warmly with whoever had spoken last.
etymology: From 'whiffle' ('to blow in gusts, vacillate'); a headword in Collins.

definition: A petty, quibbling, or unscrupulous lawyer; one who fusses over trifles.
exampleSentence: The estate was tied up for years by a pettifogger who billed for every comma.
etymology: From 'petty' + obsolete 'fogger' ('underhanded dealer'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To bully or cow someone into submission; to cringe or submit meanly.
exampleSentence: He refused to be snooled by the foreman's shouting and stood his ground.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, chiefly Scots and Northern English; a headword in Collins.

definition: Utter nonsense.
exampleSentence: "Healing crystals? What a load of codswallop," she said.
etymology: Of uncertain 20th-century British origin; a headword in Collins.

definition: Coarse, abusive, foul-mouthed language.
exampleSentence: When the deal collapsed he let loose a stream of billingsgate that cleared the room.
etymology: After Billingsgate, the old London fish market famed for its fishwives' language; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A free-for-all brawl or uproarious quarrel.
exampleSentence: The peaceful council meeting dissolved into a full donnybrook over the parking plan.
etymology: After Donnybrook, a Dublin suburb once famous for its rowdy fair; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Rumour or gossip.
exampleSentence: The office scuttlebutt was that a merger had already been signed.
etymology: Originally a ship's water cask, around which sailors gossiped; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A playful, old-fashioned word for an umbrella.
exampleSentence: "Take your bumbershoot," Grandpa called, "it's coming on to rain."
etymology: A late-19th-century American jocular alteration of 'umbrella' + 'parachute'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To make small enhancing touches to one's appearance; to spruce up.
exampleSentence: She paused to titivate her hair in the hall mirror before opening the door.
etymology: Of 19th-century origin, perhaps a fanciful formation on 'tidy'; a headword in Collins.

definition: Of, relating to, or resembling a hedgehog.
exampleSentence: With his bristly grey crewcut he had a distinctly erinaceous look.
etymology: From Latin 'erinaceus' ('hedgehog'); a headword in Collins.

definition: A passage or entrance in an amphitheatre through which crowds pour in and out.
exampleSentence: At the final whistle the fans surged out through every vomitory of the great stadium.
etymology: From Latin 'vomitorium', from 'vomere' ('to discharge'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To skip and frolic playfully.
exampleSentence: The lambs gambolled across the meadow in the first warm light of spring.
etymology: From French 'gambade' ('a leap'), from Italian 'gamba' ('leg'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To walk about leisurely; to stroll through a place.
exampleSentence: Each evening the old professor would perambulate the college gardens, hands clasped behind him.
etymology: From Latin 'perambulare' ('to walk through'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To wander or stray, whether in body or in speech; to digress.
exampleSentence: The lecture tended to divagate into long anecdotes that had nothing to do with the topic.
etymology: From Latin 'divagari' ('to wander about'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The small vertical groove running between the nose and the upper lip.
exampleSentence: A bead of sweat traced the philtrum above his lip in the heat.
etymology: From Greek 'philtron' ('love charm, dimple of the upper lip'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The smooth area of bone between the eyebrows.
exampleSentence: She frowned so often that two lines had settled permanently across her glabella.
etymology: From Latin 'glabellus' ('smooth, hairless'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A deep, bittersweet longing for someone or something absent and perhaps unattainable.
exampleSentence: The old fado song filled her with saudade for a home she had not seen in thirty years.
etymology: From Portuguese 'saudade'; naturalized into English and a headword in Collins.

definition: A light breeze that ruffles the surface of water in scattered patches.
exampleSentence: The sails hung limp until a cat's-paw darkened the bay and nudged the boat forward.
etymology: From the resemblance of the ruffled water to a cat's paw print; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A profound spiritual anguish or restless yearning, often felt without any identifiable cause.
exampleSentence: A grey toska settled over him on Sunday evenings, an ache of the soul with nothing to long for.
etymology: A Russian untranslatable; Vladimir Nabokov, in his commentary to 'Eugene Onegin' (Princeton/Bollingen, 1964), wrote that at its deepest 'toska' is 'a sensation of great spiritual anguish, often without any specific cause... a dull ache of the soul, a longing with nothing to long for.' Not yet an English dictionary headword.

definition: An aching longing for far-off places; 'farsickness,' the inverse of homesickness.
exampleSentence: Every train whistle in the night gave him a fresh pang of fernweh.
etymology: A German untranslatable ('fern' = far + 'Weh' = ache), the counterpart of 'Heimweh' (homesickness). Not yet an English dictionary headword.
